title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
description: Find the minimum steps across a grid, allowed to eliminate up to k obstacles, using BFS over a (row, col, budget) state space.

sections.title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination

content.title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination

blocks.text: Given an m x n grid where 0 marks an empty cell and 1 marks an obstacle, and an integer k, find the minimum number of steps to walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving in 4 directions. You are allowed to eliminate at most k obstacles along the way. Return -1 if it is not possible within the elimination budget.

blocks.caption: BFS expands over (row, col, eliminations used) states until the target is first reached.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Grid","m x n, grid[i][j] is 0 (empty) or 1 (obstacle)"],["Movement","4-directional, one cell per step"],["Budget","At most k obstacles may be eliminated (walked through) in total"],["Goal","Minimum steps from (0,0) to (m-1,n-1), or -1 if impossible"]]}

blocks.text: Minimum steps in an unweighted grid is a strong signal for BFS, but the twist is that a cell alone does not fully describe progress, since visiting the same cell with more remaining eliminations left is strictly better than visiting it with fewer. The state space must be expanded from (row, col) to (row, col, eliminations remaining) so BFS still explores every meaningfully distinct situation exactly once.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This extends the Open the Lock and Shortest Path in Binary Matrix pattern of "BFS over an implicit state graph" by adding a resource-budget dimension to the state.

Picture a hiker with a limited number of dynamite sticks. Each boulder blocking the trail can be blown up, but only if a stick remains. The hiker wants to reach the destination in as few steps as possible, choosing wisely when to spend a precious stick versus taking a longer route around a boulder.

blocks.caption: Dynamite clears a boulder but permanently consumes part of the limited budget.

items: Walking onto an obstacle cell costs one elimination from the budget; walking onto an empty cell costs nothing.
The same cell can be worth revisiting if reached with strictly more eliminations remaining than any prior visit, since that opens up options a prior visit could not afford.
If k is already at least m + n - 2 (the minimum possible path length under no obstacles), every obstacle on the shortest direct path could be eliminated, so the answer is simply m + n - 2.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The target (4,2) is first reached at BFS layer 6, so the answer is 6, matching the expected output. The second official example, grid = [[0,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,0]] with k = 1, has no path within the budget, so its answer is -1.

A direct BFS over just (row, col) fails here because whether a path is viable depends on how many eliminations it has already spent, not just which cell it is on. Two paths reaching the same cell with different remaining budgets are genuinely different situations.

Extend the visited set to track (row, col, eliminations remaining) instead of just (row, col). A cell is worth revisiting only if the new arrival has a remaining budget never seen before at that cell, since a state with fewer remaining eliminations is dominated by (strictly worse than or equal to) an earlier visit with more remaining eliminations at the same step count or better.
BFS over (row, col, eliminations remaining) states using a general hash-set for visited, without capping k first. This is correct but can track more states than necessary when k is very large.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(m * n * k)","Each of up to m*n*k distinct states is visited once, each with O(1) neighbor expansion"],["Space","O(m * n * k)","Hash-set visited states, plus the BFS queue"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: When k is very large (larger than the grid actually needs), the state space is bigger than necessary, since no shortest path ever needs more than m + n - 2 eliminations.

Cap k at m + n - 2 before starting BFS, since no shortest path can possibly need more eliminations than the length of the shortest possible unobstructed path. This bounds the state space to O(m * n * (m + n)) in the worst case and lets visited be a fixed-size 3D boolean array instead of a hash-set, which is both faster and simpler. BFS layer by layer (processing one full frontier per step) makes the step count implicit in the loop, avoiding the need to store distance in each queue entry.

items: Cap k = min(k, m + n - 2) up front.
Use a 3D visited array indexed by (row, col, eliminations remaining).
BFS layer by layer; the layer index directly is the step count when the target is first reached.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, uncapped hash-set BFS","O(m * n * k)","O(m * n * k)"],["Optimized, capped array-based BFS","O(m * n * (m + n))","O(m * n * (m + n))"]]}

items: When a resource budget affects which moves are valid, fold it into the BFS state alongside position.
Cap a budget parameter at the theoretical maximum useful value (here, the unobstructed shortest path length) to bound the state space tightly.
BFS layer by layer naturally tracks distance without storing it explicitly in each state.

blocks.text: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination extends plain grid BFS by including the remaining elimination budget as part of the state, since the same cell can be a genuinely different situation depending on how much budget is left. Capping k at m + n - 2 keeps the state space tight, and layer-by-layer BFS finds the minimum number of steps, or determines the target is unreachable within budget.
